file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to launch a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that:

| Requirement | Example |
|-------------|---------|
| **GPU** | NVIDIA RTX A6000 (`nvidia-a6000`) |
| **OS** | Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (Focal) |
| **Machine type** | `n1-standard-8` (8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM) – you can change this to suit your workload |
| **Zone** | `us-central1-a` (pick any zone that supports GPUs) |
| **Project** | `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` (replace with your actual GCP project ID) |

> **NOTE**  
> * Google Cloud does **not** use the term “EC2”; that’s AWS terminology.  
> * You must have **GPU quota** for the chosen zone and **billing enabled**.  
> * The GPU must be attached to a **machine type that supports GPUs** (e.g., `n1-standard-8`, `n1-highmem-8`, `n1-highcpu-8`, etc.).  
> * The GPU image must be **pre‑installed** with NVIDIA drivers. The Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image from the official Google Cloud Marketplace already includes the drivers.

---

## 1. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# 1️⃣  Authenticate (if you haven’t already)
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID

# 2️⃣  Enable the Compute Engine API (once per project)
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com

# 3️⃣  Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create rtx-a6000-ubuntu \
  --zone us-central1-a \
  --machine-type n1-standard-8 \
  --accelerator type=nvidia-a6000,count=1 \
  --image-family ubuntu-2004-lts \
  --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud \
  --boot-disk-size 100GB \
  --boot-disk-type pd-ssd \
  --metadata startup-script='#!/bin/bash
    # Optional: update & install packages
    apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y
    # Install CUDA toolkit (if needed)
    apt-get install -y cuda-toolkit-11-8
  ' \
  --tags http-server,https-server \
  --scopes compute-rw,storage-ro
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--zone` | The zone where the instance will live. |
| `--machine-type` | CPU & RAM allocation. |
| `--accelerator` | Attaches the GPU. |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Pulls the Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image that already contains NVIDIA drivers. |
| `--boot-disk-size` & `--boot-disk-type` | SSD for fast I/O. |
| `--metadata startup-script` | Optional shell script that runs on first boot (e.g., install CUDA). |
| `--tags` | Network tags for firewall rules. |
| `--scopes` | IAM scopes for the instance. |

> **Tip:** If you need a different machine type, just replace `n1-standard-8` with something like `n1-highmem-8` or `n1-highcpu-8`.

---

## 2. Using the REST API (curl)

If you prefer to use the raw REST API, here’s a minimal example.  
You’ll need an OAuth 2.0 access token with the `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/compute` scope.

```bash
# 1️⃣  Get an access token (replace with your own method)
ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)

# 2️⃣  Define variables
PROJECT="YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
ZONE="us-central1-a"
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"

# 3️⃣  Build the JSON payload
cat <<EOF > instance.json
{
  "name": "$INSTANCE_NAME",
  "machineType": "zones/$ZONE/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "projects/$PROJECT/zones/$ZONE/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "accelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorType": "projects/$PROJECT/zones/$ZONE/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-a6000",
      "acceleratorCount": 1
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\\napt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  }
}
EOF

# 4️⃣  POST the request
curl -X POST \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/$PROJECT/zones/$ZONE/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @instance.json
```

### Explanation of the JSON

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `name` | Instance name |
| `machineType` | Full path to the machine type |
| `disks` | Boot disk configuration (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image, 100 GB SSD) |
| `networkInterfaces` | Default VPC with external NAT |
| `accelerators` | Attach one RTX A6000 GPU |
| `metadata` | Startup script (optional) |
| `tags` | Network tags for firewall rules |

> **Important:**  
> * The `acceleratorType` path must match the zone (`nvidia-a6000`).  
> * If you need more than one GPU, set `"acceleratorCount": 2` (or more).  
> * Ensure you have the necessary GPU quota in the chosen zone.

---

## 3. Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✔️  Verify GPU quota for `nvidia-a6000` in your zone. |
| ✔️  Enable Compute Engine API. |
| ✔️  Ensure billing is active. |
| ✔️  Use an image that includes NVIDIA drivers (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS from `ubuntu-os-cloud`). |
| ✔️  Attach the GPU with `--accelerator` (CLI) or `accelerators` (REST). |
| ✔️  Set appropriate firewall rules (e.g., allow SSH, HTTP/HTTPS). |
| ✔️  Optionally add a startup script to install CUDA or other libraries. |

---

### Final Note

Once the instance is running, you can SSH into it:

```bash
gcloud compute ssh rtx-a6000-ubuntu --zone us-central1-a
```

From there, you can verify the GPU:

```bash
nvidia-smi
```

You should see the RTX A6000 listed with its driver version. Happy GPU computing!
